newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Central Asian spring rites turn back on Soviet era.
newsitem.headline: Central Asian spring rites turn back on Soviet era.

text.p: The countries of Central Asia made a colourful return to an ancient tradition from their pre-Soviet past on Friday in festivities marking the Navruz or "new days" spring holiday.
Navruz, a Moslem adaptation of pre-Islamic celebrations for the coming of spring, was prohibited by the Soviets in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Moslem families celebrated the ancient holiday regardless behind closed doors.
In the Uzbek capital Tashkent on Friday, the aroma of pilau, the spicy national dish made from rice and mutton, wafted from dozens of cauldrons sitting in the streets of the city centre.
"Today, on this spring holiday, I've prepared a real delicacy and added raisins to the pilau," said one of several cheerful cooks on the streets of Tashkent.
Soviet-style slogans, evidence of the holiday's new official blessing, declared: "Navruz -- a holiday of friendship and kindness."

Crowds thronged the main street between Tashkent's Independence Square and the recently completed monument to the region's 14th century Mongol ruler, Tamerlane. Until recently, Karl Marx glowered at passers-by on the same spot.
"Our independence has returned this festivity to us alongside many other ancient eastern traditions," the official daily Pravda Vostoka trumpeted.
Uzbekistan is officially a secular state and its strongman president, Islam Karimov, is deeply suspicious of radical Islam in nearby Iran and Afghanistan.
But according to the weekly Central Asian Post, the 23-million population have been busy building and restoring the country's mosques.

"In the days of Soviet power there were 80 mosques in the republic...after independence their number has risen to nearly 5,000," the weekly said. In neighbouring Kazakhstan, with old nomadic traditions, Navruz is also a time to play "qyz quu", a chase on horseback between a boy and a girl.
If the boy catches the girl, he wins a kiss -- if the girl catches the boy, she gets to whip him with her riding crop.
But hard-hit by a painful economic transition, many in Tashkent felt they have little to celebrate. Monthly wages, if they are paid, average $20-$30 a month across the region.
There was a large police presence in Tashkent on Friday. Karimov tolerates little dissent.
"Reviving our traditions is a good thing," said one Uzbek who declined to be identified. "But it would have been better to give the money spent on these festivities to the poor," he said.
